Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

issues.item: Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile: darkness and especially tactile/unexpected touch are more characteristic of direct interpersonal assault than of a loved-one trauma, and there is no accompanying memory or appraisal content that links touch or darkness to this trauma.

The lock-checking threat item and parallel checking-locks strategy suggest a home-intrusion or direct personal danger formulation. In a loved-one trauma profile, this can occur, but here it is not supported by any appraisals or memory content about preventing another loss, danger to family, or responsibility. As selected, these items pull toward a different trauma narrative than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Within the allowed nodes, the strongest coherence is around hyperarousal and intrusive memory, but the specific combination of tactile triggers plus lock-checking behavior is difficult to explain as one coherent formulation for a loved-one trauma without any linked negative appraisal content. This is more than merely unusual because the selected items imply different threat contexts.

The trigger/threat pattern is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of trauma to a loved one. Tactile unexpected-touch triggers plus broad startle to nearby movement are more typical of direct assault or personal threat trauma, not bereavement-focused trauma, unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Door/lock checking and hypervigilant startle responses imply an ongoing fear of intruders or immediate physical attack, but the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory and loss-related trigger content rather than a coherent physical-danger narrative tied to the loved-one trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, but the selected threat items reflect personal safety/intruder danger whereas the only clearly trauma-congruent trigger is loss-themed conversation. This creates a poor match between the active nodes: the threat content does not plausibly arise from the listed trauma-relevant triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, tactile triggering by unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a direct personal-assault or physical-threat theme that is not supported by the memory items or the loss-focused trigger item. This makes the trigger set clinically incoherent around the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window lock checking suggests an ongoing home-intrusion or personal safety threat appraisal. In a profile centered on trauma to a loved one, with memory items focused on reliving and no appraisals linking the event to current intruder danger, this threat item does not fit the dominant loss-based formulation and appears mismatched with the other selected items.

issues.item: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeatedly checking locks/doors/windows is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the indexed trauma type (trauma to a loved one). The other selected items center on grief/loss reminders, intrusive vivid replay, and generalized startle, but do not indicate a home-intrusion, assault, or safety-compulsion theme that would make lock-checking a coherent trauma-linked strategy. As selected, this item appears to target a threat-management pattern not otherwise represented in triggers, memory, or appraisals.

vignette: When his mother collapsed on the kitchen table one humid summer night, the world narrowed to a single, suffocating image of a hand clutching a trembling throat. The funeral's soft music, the black lilies on the casket, the scent of embalming fluid-each became a quiet echo that would later resurface in the most ordinary moments. In his shop, the moment a regular customer mentioned "the loss of a brother" or a neighbor's wife lamented the death of a child, the memories surged forward, as if the past had broken its own boundaries. These conversations and the sight of a funeral wreath at a community gathering did not merely remind him of loss; they stirred the same startle reflexes that had erupted when his mother's heart stopped, and the sudden creak of a closing door or a distant car horn made his chest tighten with a fresh wave of fear. In that instant, the triggers, the memories of a sudden, violent end, and the threat of a new danger intertwined, re-awakening the terror that had been buried beneath his grief. The memory of the night he held his mother's hand for the last time, the clarity of the light filtering through the kitchen window, the exact sound of her breath stalling-this image has taken on the immediacy of a present event, as if the scene is still unfolding. Whenever he closes his eyes to quiet the noise of his shop, that vivid film plays over and over, each frame as sharp as the last. The panic that rises from that replay, the startle response to ordinary sounds, the shame he feels at watching himself recoil-these are the threats that drive him to the nearest cigarette after closing his shop. Smoking, he believes, is a way to silence the memory's roar, to give his mind a brief reprieve from the relentless intrusions. He also avoids any thoughts about that night, closing the conversation with customers about "family stuff" as if touching on the topic would summon the image back. The avoidance, the smoking, and the instinct to keep the memory at bay become a cycle of self-preservation that feeds on the same fear he once fought. As the years stretched, the cigarette's smoke became a crutch that tethered him to his trauma. When he stepped out for a break, the nicotine hit his lungs, the brief calm it produced briefly muted the startle, only for the relief to vanish and the threat to surge again. The more he turned to smoking to quell the memory, the more the memory grew vivid, its scenes replaying with sharper detail whenever he tried to avoid them. The avoidance of grief reminders-never walking past the memorial garden behind the church, never listening to a radio program about recent tragedies-meant that when those triggers finally slipped past his vigilance, they struck him with an even stronger force. The startle to a sudden movement in the shop, the scream of a customer startled by a loose shelf, would bring the same terror he felt on that kitchen table, and the smoke that night would only deepen the looping sense that his mind was stuck in a never-ending replay. The shop that once thrummed with the rhythm of daily commerce now feels like a silent echo chamber. He keeps the windows closed when he hears customers discuss their own losses, fearing the sound of a funeral announcement on the radio would set his heart racing. His avoidance has begun to erode his relationships: the wife who once smiled at his jokes now watches him in a mix of pity and irritation, seeing the way he fumbles his words when grief enters the conversation. He has cut back on social interactions, preferring the solitude of the back room where he can control the noise and light. The smoking has left its mark on his hands and his breath, a constant reminder of the ritual he uses to tether himself to safety. The startle to ordinary sounds has become so ingrained that a passing car horn can send him scrambling to the back door, a reflex that costs him time and, in the long run, his business's reputation. It was the day he missed a customer's birthday because the phone rang and he bolted for the back, coughing and heart racing, that he finally reached for help. He is terrified that the cycle will consume his life entirely, that the memory will always feel present, that the startle responses will one day kill him as they killed his mother. Yet, he also clings to the hope that with intervention he can break the chain, to let the image of his mother's last breath be a memory, not a present terror, and to reclaim the quiet in his shop, in his home, and in himself.
